## User requirements
The user asked for: **Target: AAAI 2026
Track: AI Alignment / Main Technical Track — Robustness Evaluation

Direction: Build an end-to-end framework (CRADE) that jointly profiles per-instance contamination, generates adversarial functional variants with provable correctness, evaluates reasoning at the step level, and produces IRT-calibrated "genuine capability" scores that decompose observed performance into true ability, contamination boost, and robustness deficit. The core insight is that contamination and robustness are entangled — a model may fail perturbations because it memorized answers OR because it lacks genuine reasoning, and disentangling these requires joint modeling that no existing work provides.

Seed Papers:
- Zawalski et al. "CoDeC" (NVIDIA, arXiv 2025) — Gray-box contamination detection at 99.9% AUC; provides the detection backbone but produces no corrective evaluation
- Li et al. "ATLAS" (arXiv 2025) — IRT-based adaptive testing achieving 90% item reduction; demonstrates IRT's power for LLM evaluation but assumes test integrity
- Hou et al. "MaSTer" (arXiv 2026) — Automated adversarial math variant generation with 48% accuracy reduction; best current perturbation method but disconnected from contamination
- Zheng et al. "ReasoningMath-Plus" (arXiv 2026) — Step-level evaluation showing answer-level overestimates by ~1.4 points; proves process-level matters but lacks adversarial component
- Chen et al. "Reasoning Models Don't Always Say What They Think" (Anthropic, May 2025) — CoT faithfulness is only 25% for hint disclosure; establishes that CoT is unreliable but doesn't connect to contamination
- Xu et al. "DCR" (arXiv 2025) — Contamination-adjusted scores via fuzzy inference; closest competitor but lacks IRT grounding, variant generation, and process-level analysis
- Kocetkov et al. "On The Fragility of Benchmark Contamination Detection in Reasoning Models" (arXiv Oct 2025) — Shows detection fails for reasoning models; establishes urgent need for new approaches

Known Gaps:
- No framework jointly estimates contamination level, generates adversarial variants, and produces a single calibrated capability score (existing work addresses these in isolation)
- Step-level perturbation alignment (whether CoT appropriately tracks problem changes) has never been measured or connected to contamination — all adversarial work evaluates final answers only
- Item Response Theory for LLM evaluation (ATLAS, PSN-IRT) assumes zero contamination; contamination-aware IRT with joint ability-contamination estimation is entirely missing
- Existing contamination detection fails on reasoning models (near random-guess), creating demand for process-level and faithfulness-based alternatives

Theoretical Anchor: Contamination-aware 3PL IRT model: P(correct | θ_j, d_i, c_ij) = c_ij · p_mem + (1 - c_ij) · σ(θ_j - d_i), with EM-based joint estimation of ability θ, difficulty d, and contamination indicators c. The decomposition Observed_accuracy = G + C - R (genuine capability + contamination boost - robustness deficit) provides a formal framework grounded in measurement theory.

Constraints:
- Compute: ≤200 H100-hours (estimated ~120 for combined RQ1+RQ2)
- Timeline: 8-10 weeks to AAAI deadline (abstract July 25, paper August 1)
- Must validate calibrated scores against MathArena's uncontaminated 2025 competition data as ground truth

Quality Self-Checks:
- [x] Core insight: "Contamination and robustness are entangled — you can't measure one without accounting for the other, and disentangling them requires joint modeling at the reasoning-step level."
- [x] Why not obvious: The contamination-detection and adversarial-robustness communities are separate research streams with different venues and different authors; the IRT-for-LLMs community is a third silo. Nobody sits at the three-way intersection. DCR Factor shows the field is approaching this but only from the detection+adjustment angle.
- [x] Baseline fear test: A simple baseline of "run on variants and average" loses the contamination-robustness decomposition and the step-level memorization signatures — the calibrated IRT score and process-level SPA metric are what differentiate.
- [x] Information exploited: Per-instance contamination profiles crossed with per-variant step-level reasoning chain changes — no existing method uses this joint signal.

Avoid:
- Pure contamination detection without corrective evaluation (saturated space with 5+ strong methods)
- Yet another dynamic benchmark (LiveBench, MathArena, DyVal already exist) — this must be a framework applicable to ANY existing benchmark
- Ad-hoc perturbation studies on single benchmarks without methodological/theoretical contribution (GSM-Plus, GSM-Symbolic, MATH-Perturb already cover this)
- Using LLMs in the variant generation loop (creates circular dependency and unverifiable correctness) — use SymPy-backed symbolic generation instead**
Evaluate whether this idea actually meets the user's requirements. An idea that doesn't match should be "revise" or "fail".

## Feasibility Verification Report

### 1. NumPyro/Stan for Bayesian IRT at Small N

**Verdict: FEASIBLE -- well-supported by literature and existing implementations.**

A peer-reviewed study directly compares PyStan and NumPyro for Bayesian IRT (both 1PL and 2PL models): Comparison between pystan and numpyro in Bayesian item response theory (PeerJ Computer Science, 2023). Key findings:
- Both frameworks produce equivalent parameter estimates for 2PL-IRT models.
- NumPyro is generally faster than PyStan, especially with GPU acceleration on large datasets.
- Both use the NUTS sampler successfully.

For the small-N regime (15-20 examinees x 1000+ items), Stan has a dedicated hierarchical 2PL example model in its official repository, and there is a published study specifically on "An Optimized Bayesian Hierarchical Two-Parameter Logistic Model for Small-Sample Item Calibration" (Konig, Spoden, Frey, 2020) that addresses exactly this concern. The paper notes that while standard 2PL typically requires 500+ respondents, hierarchical Bayesian priors substantially reduce sample size requirements. The N=15-20 regime is small even for hierarchical approaches, but the proposal's use case (1000+ items per examinee) provides dense data per subject, which helps identification. This is feasible but the proposal should acknowledge convergence diagnostics will be critical.

### 2. py-irt Library

**Verdict: EXISTS and is suitable.**

py-irt is a real, published library: [py-irt: A Scalable Item Response Theory Library for Python](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01282), published in INFORMS Journal on Computing (Vol 35, No 1, 2023). GitHub: [nd-ball/py-irt](https://github.com/nd-ball/py-irt).

Key confirmed features:
- Built on Pyro/PyTorch with GPU acceleration.
- Supports variational inference (this is its primary estimation method).
- Implements 1PL, 2PL, and 4PL models.
- Supports both vague and hierarchical priors.
- Designed explicitly for large-scale IRT fitting (it was the first Python package for this purpose).

This would handle the proposed scale (15-20 examinees x 1000+ items) well via variational inference.

### 3. SymPy for Math Problem Verification

**Verdict: FEASIBLE for algebraic/arithmetic problems, with important caveats.**

SymPy can verify math answers through symbolic comparison (e.g., `sp.simplify(answer - correct_answer) == 0`). The SymCode paper (2025) demonstrates a systematic pipeline: identify calculation steps, generate SymPy verification scripts, execute in sandbox, and compare outputs.

**Strengths**: Algebra, calculus, equation solving, numerical computation, matrix operations -- all well-suited for GSM8K-style math problems.

**Limitations** (important for the proposal):
- Synthetic geometry proofs -- SymPy cannot handle abstract geometric reasoning.
- Proof by induction or contradiction -- not formalizable symbolically.
- Combinatorial arguments that resist symbolic formalization.
- Problems requiring semantic/word-problem interpretation before symbolic encoding still need an LLM or human to set up the SymPy expression.

For verifying adversarial **variants** of GSM8K-style grade-school math (arithmetic, algebra, basic word problems), SymPy is well-suited. The proposal should note that verification coverage will not be 100% -- some problem types will require manual or LLM-assisted verification.

### 4. Open LLM Leaderboard V1 GSM8K Data Assembly via tinyBenchmarks

**Verdict: METHODOLOGY EXISTS, but assembly requires work.**

The tinyBenchmarks paper (Polo, Weber, Choshen, Sun, Xu, Yurochkin; ICML 2024) is confirmed real and published. Key facts:
- The paper uses per-item correctness data from the Open LLM Leaderboard V1, including GSM8K.

The methodology for assembling per-item response matrices from V1 data has indeed been demonstrated. Reconstructing the full matrix from V1 submissions would require re-running models or accessing cached outputs, which is non-trivial.

### 5. OLMo-2-13B Fine-tuning

**Verdict: MODEL EXISTS. ~5 H100-hours is plausible for limited fine-tuning.**

OLMo-2-13B is confirmed real, released by AI2 (Allen Institute for AI) in November 2024. It is available on HuggingFace (`allenai/OLMo-2-1124-13B` and `allenai/OLMo-2-1124-13B-Instruct`). Key facts:
- Fully open-source (weights, training data, code, recipes, logs, intermediate checkpoints).

For "synthetic contamination" fine-tuning (presumably fine-tuning on benchmark answers to simulate contamination), ~5 H100-hours is plausible if using LoRA/QLoRA on a modest dataset. Full fine-tuning on a large dataset would require more, but for contamination simulation (likely a small dataset of benchmark items), this estimate is reasonable.

It is a 27B dense model with 262K token context, multimodal capabilities (text, image, video), and strong coding performance (outperforms the much larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B on coding benchmarks).
